protocol.scope_summary: EACPP clinical practice guideline for oral health risk assessment and fluoride varnish application, 'Service recommended for patients aged 18 months and over' (p.1). Flow: meet service and professional obligations -> obtain patient history and complete assessment (patient/dental history, risk assessment, visual screening using the 'lift the lip' technique) -> confirm management is appropriate (contraindications, precautions, interactions, pregnancy and lactation per Queensland Health Guideline QH-GDL-410:2013 and manufacturer product information) -> explain treatment and apply fluoride varnish (Duraphat® 5 per cent w/v sodium fluoride varnish; recommended twice per year, up to 4 applications per year at higher risk) -> provide general and preventative advice (post-application instructions, toothbrushing advice by age band). 'Refer when' (p.3) defines immediate (same day), urgent (within 3 days) and routine referral triggers; 'Treat (if clinically appropriate) and concurrently refer' (p.3) defines conditions treated while referring. Appendices supply risk assessment/screening tools (18 months to 5 years; ≥6 years), clinical photographs and the Duraphat® application procedure with age/dentition dose bands. Ineligibility for the prescribing service does not preclude usual pharmacy care.

inclusion.text: Service recommended for patients aged 18 months and over.

This clinical practice guideline may only be used by pharmacists who have been approved by the Department of Health to participate in the Enhanced Access Community Pharmacy Pilot (EACPP) and are authorised to prescribe under the Medicines and Poisons Regulations 2016 (WA). This document alone does not provide an authorisation for a pharmacist to prescribe.
Initial patient eligibility and suitability for management within the scope of the service
Patient informed consent (including consent for communication with other health practitioners if relevant)
Patients may either be referred by a dental practitioner (an oral health therapist, dental therapist, oral hygienist, or dentist)
or assessed by the pharmacist as at moderate or high risk of tooth decay or poor oral health and be eligible for fluoride varnish application

exclusion.text: the patient is aged below 18 months (does not preclude a patient from accessing usual pharmacy care)
the patient is screened at high or moderate risk of tooth decay/poor oral health but the application of fluoride varnish is contraindicated
immediate (same day) referral required: recent orofacial trauma (not yet seen by a dental and/or medical practitioner)
facial swelling or fever from an oral infection
a toothache that is worsening despite taking regular analgesia
urgent (within 3 days) referral required: advanced decay (discolouration and cavitation)
a toothache that is not impacting daily functioning and can be managed with over-the-counter analgesics.

Where there is any doubt about the suitability of a patient, the pharmacist should not undertake the procedure and refer the patient to their preferred dental practitioner, closest public dental service, or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Community Controlled dental clinic.

exclusion_exceptions.text: Ineligibility for treatment as part of a prescribing service does not preclude a patient from accessing services provided as part of usual pharmacy care.

diagnosis_pathways.name: Oral health risk assessment and fluoride application - guideline overview pathway (page 2 flow, elaborated pages 4-7)

steps.description: Meet service and professional obligations: initial patient eligibility and suitability for management within the scope of the service; patient informed consent (including consent for communication with other health practitioners if relevant).

gates.criterion: Initial patient eligibility and suitability for management within the scope of the service (Refer when: the patient is aged below 18 months)
Patient informed consent (including consent for communication with other health practitioners if relevant)

steps.description: Obtain patient history and complete assessment: 'To assess the patient's suitability for an application of fluoride varnish and/or whether a referral to a dental practitioner or another appropriate healthcare provider is required, an oral health risk assessment, patient history, and dental history must be undertaken by the pharmacist. Fluoride varnish should be considered for patients aged 18 months and over.' Review for other signs and symptoms that may require the attention of another healthcare provider (see Refer when) and consider standard pharmacy treatment and referral where appropriate (e.g. for mouth ulcers). Appendix 2 provides descriptions and clinical photographs of common oral presentations.

gates.criterion: Consider referring to a dental practitioner if the child is not able to co-operate with visual screening (e.g. unwilling/unable to show you their mouth or stay still enough for assessment)

provenance.section_heading: Obtain patient history and complete assessment

steps.description: Patient history: consider age; pregnancy and lactation status (if applicable); current medical conditions or special healthcare needs that may impact on oral health status and the safe use of fluoride varnish, e.g. asthma (severity and current level of symptom control), history of hospitalisation for allergic reactions; current illness e.g. colds, influenza, current infection of herpes simplex virus (HSV); current and recently ceased treatments (including prescribed medicines, vitamins, herbs, other supplements, and over-the-counter medicines); drug allergies/adverse drug reactions; hypersensitivity/allergic reaction to colophony (natural resin) e.g. sticking plasters or medical adhesives; smoking status (including vaping). Dental history: does the patient have a dental practitioner that they visit routinely?; when did the patient last see a dental practitioner? What was the reason e.g. emergency treatment, toothache, routine check-up?; when was the last fluoride varnish application? Any previous adverse experiences with fluoride varnish?; history of recent orofacial trauma (within the last 6 months), oral infections, toothaches, or other oral pain (including use of analgesics), soft tissue pathology in or around the mouth (ulcerative gingivitis, herpetic stomatitis, or aphthous ulcers), tooth discolouration; impacts of oral health on quality of life including sleep and school attendance; oral hygiene routines including type of toothbrush, toothpaste fluoride strength, toothbrushing frequency, use of fluoridated products, other oral hygiene aids; consumption of fluoridated water. Reminder: Pharmacists can access a range of clinical information in a patient's My Health Record, including details about current and past medication history, allergies, and current medical conditions.

gates.criterion: Refer when: recent orofacial trauma (not yet seen by a dental and/or medical practitioner)

steps.description: Risk assessment and screening: 'There is no arbitrary scoring system for risk status due to the variability of the interaction between risk factors and protective factors. Pharmacists must use their professional judgement to evaluate a child's risk status.' A child with no obvious clinical signs of decay, only a few moderate level risk factors, and multiple protective factors may be deemed low risk. If the child has at least one high risk factor, regardless of the number of protective factors, they would be at least at moderate risk of tooth decay and poor oral health, and fluoride varnish application should be considered. For patients aged 6 years and over, a risk assessment questionnaire is completed with the patient, and/or parent/caregiver. Risk assessment tools: Appendix 1 (18 months to 5 years) and Appendix 3 (≥6 years). Visual screening using the 'lift the lip' technique is recommended for patients aged 18 months to 5 years; lift the lip may not be required as anterior caries are less common for patients aged 6 years and over, as signs of poor oral health may be easily observable, such as plaque accumulation, decay, abscess, trauma, gingivitis, or bad breath. During the screening, the pharmacist should look for: signs of tooth decay (white spot lesions, brown spot lesions, cavitation (holes)); facial trauma (loose or broken teeth, lacerations on gums); oral infection, facial swelling/asymmetry due to spreading infection; gum disease (red, swollen gums); other relevant findings including mouth ulcers and possible signs of fluorosis.

gates.criterion: The patient is screened at high or moderate risk of tooth decay/poor oral health (required before fluoride varnish application; the document does not state the action for a low-risk patient)
Consider referring to a dental practitioner if the child is not able to co-operate with visual screening
Routine referral to a dental practitioner (including public dental clinic) is required if the child has not had a dental check-up (not just emergency treatment) in the past 12 months

steps.description: Confirm management is appropriate: 'Refer to the Queensland Health Guideline for Fluoride Varnish (QH-GDL-410:2013) and specific product information provided by the manufacturer to confirm the application of fluoride varnish is appropriate, including: contraindications and precautions; drug interactions; pregnancy and lactation.' General information only is provided within this guideline. Where there is any doubt about the suitability of a patient, the pharmacist should not undertake the procedure and refer the patient to their preferred dental practitioner, closest public dental service, or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Community Controlled dental clinic.

gates.criterion: Contraindications and precautions to fluoride varnish application
Where there is any doubt about the suitability of a patient
Pregnancy and lactation (confirm application is appropriate per QH-GDL-410:2013 and product information)

steps.description: Explain treatment and apply fluoride varnish: discuss treatment - application procedure, recommended frequency, what to expect, adverse effects, post-application instructions; Duraphat® application (Appendix 4). Advise patients and/or parents/caregivers that fluoride varnish is a preventative treatment and cannot reverse advanced tooth decay (although it may halt further development), treat dental infections, or relieve dental pain. An 'at-risk' tooth surface is defined as: a tooth surface that has signs of early decay (white spot or brown spot lesions); a tooth surface directly abutting a decayed tooth surface (in between 2 teeth); the 4 front primary teeth in the upper jaw (present in children up to age of 6 to 7 years) - apply to outside (front), inside (back), and biting surfaces; chewing (occlusal) surfaces and interproximal surfaces (in between) of molars and pre-molars (if present). The recommended frequency of fluoride varnish application is twice per year; more frequent applications (up to 4 applications per year) are recommended for patients at higher risk of dental caries.

gates.criterion: The patient is screened at high or moderate risk of tooth decay/poor oral health
Treat and concurrently refer: the patient presents with white spot lesions or advancing decay (brown spot lesions – no cavitation evident)
Treat and concurrently refer: the patient has not seen a dental practitioner in the previous 12 months.

Refer when: immediate (same day) referral required - recent orofacial trauma; facial swelling or fever from an oral infection; difficulty swallowing or breathing; a toothache that is worsening despite taking regular analgesia

Refer when: urgent (within 3 days) referral required - advanced decay (discolouration and cavitation); a visible abscess; a toothache that is not impacting daily functioning and can be managed with over-the-counter analgesics

provenance.section_heading: Explain treatment and apply fluoride varnish

steps.description: Post application instructions and provide general and preventative advice: provide patients and/or parents/caregiver with post-application instructions and advice before the procedure is undertaken - eating and drinking should be avoided for at least 30 minutes after application, after which time soft food and fluids can be consumed; not to chew food (i.e. harder foods) for at least 4 hours after application; not to brush teeth for at least 4 hours after application. The efficacy of fluoride varnish depends on the length of time it can remain undisturbed on the teeth surfaces. Patients and/or parents/caregivers should be reminded of the importance of regular check-ups with a dental practitioner and provided with appropriate information to enable effective home care. The application of fluoride varnish should be documented and communicated to the patient's dental practitioner to avoid duplication of treatment. Anticipatory guidance should include instruction on toothbrushing, flossing, and the use of other oral hygiene aids tailored to the patient's age. Children aged 18 months to 5 years: teeth should be cleaned twice daily by a parent/caregiver with a pea sized amount of toothpaste (containing 500 to 550 ppm fluoride) using a small, soft bristled toothbrush; the child should be instructed to spit out, and not swallow the toothpaste, and not to rinse after brushing. People aged ≥6 years: teeth should be cleaned twice daily (or more frequently) with a soft bristled toothbrush and a toothpaste containing 1000 to 1500 ppm fluoride; toothpaste should not be swallowed, and the patient should avoid rinsing after brushing; floss should be used to clean in between teeth; plaque disclosing tablets may be used to demonstrate effective methods of plaque removal.

Re-application / clinical review: 'The recommended frequency of fluoride varnish application is twice per year. More frequent applications (up to 4 applications per year) are recommended for patients at higher risk of dental caries.' The application of fluoride varnish should be documented and communicated to the patient's dental practitioner to avoid duplication of treatment; patients and/or parents/caregivers should be reminded of the importance of regular check-ups with a dental practitioner.

gates.criterion: Patients at higher risk of dental caries - more frequent applications (up to 4 applications per year)

provenance.section_heading: Explain treatment and apply fluoride varnish

treatments.drug: Duraphat® 5 per cent w/v sodium fluoride varnish
treatments.form: varnish (single dose (0.4 ml) pack or multi dose tube)
treatments.strength: 5 per cent w/v sodium fluoride varnish
treatments.dose: As per the manufacturer's instructions for use, the dose of Duraphat® varies based on age (and subsequently, dentition type): young children with primary teeth only: up to 0.25 mL Duraphat® (5.6 mg fluoride); older children with mixed dentition: up to 0.4 mL Duraphat® (9.04 mg fluoride); adolescents and adults with permanent dentition: up to 0.75 mL Duraphat® (16.95 mg fluoride).
treatments.route: topical (applied directly to at-risk tooth surfaces)
treatments.frequency: twice per year; more frequent applications (up to 4 applications per year) are recommended for patients at higher risk of dental caries (p.6)
treatments.max_dose: Adolescents and adults with permanent dentition: up to 0.75 mL Duraphat® (16.95 mg fluoride). Age/dentition maxima: up to 0.25 mL (5.6 mg fluoride) primary teeth only; up to 0.4 mL (9.04 mg fluoride) mixed dentition.
treatments.notes: Strength context (p.3): 'Fluoride varnish contains 22.6 mg/mL (22,600 ppm) fluoride ion suspended in an alcohol and resin base. The only fluoride varnish currently registered in Australia to prevent caries is Duraphat® 5 per cent w/v sodium fluoride varnish.' Dose (p.12): 'A single use Duraphat® Dosage Pad that indicates the amount of fluoride to be applied or Duraphat® Varnish Single Dose (0.4 mL) must be used to ensure the correct amount of varnish is dispensed and applied.' Equipment (p.12): Duraphat® varnish (single dose (0.4 ml) pack or multi dose tube); Duraphat® dosage pad; cotton gauze; disposable microbrush/applicator; PPE (gloves, protective eyewear, single use surgical mask, apron (optional)); single use, self-adhesive bib; clean dry soft-bristle toothbrush (optional). Application (p.12-13): thin layer to 2 to 3 teeth in one quadrant at a time, starting with the upper front teeth, moving to the back, then lower teeth; for restless young children prioritise the upper front teeth. Contraindication-within-protocol (p.5): 'Where there is any doubt about the suitability of a patient, the pharmacist should not undertake the procedure and refer the patient to their preferred dental practitioner, closest public dental service, or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Community Controlled dental clinic.' Scope limit (p.13): 'Duraphat® is indicated as a spot application fluoride treatment for at-risk tooth surfaces. It should not be applied to the whole dentition in one session (systemic treatment).' Adverse effects (p.6): 'In rare cases swelling of the oral mucosa, ulcerative gingivitis, and stomatitis has been observed in sensitive individuals and/or those with a tendency to allergic reactions.'; 'Teeth may appear yellow for up to 24 hours due to the tint of the varnish, before it wears off and tooth colour returns to normal.'; 'There is no published evidence that professional application of fluoride varnish is a risk factor for enamel fluorosis in children of any age.' Pregnancy/lactation caveat (p.5): confirm management is appropriate including 'contraindications and precautions; drug interactions; pregnancy and lactation' per Queensland Health Guideline for Fluoride Varnish (QH-GDL-410:2013) and manufacturer product information; 'General information only is provided within this guideline.' Post-application instructions (p.7): eating and drinking avoided for at least 30 minutes; no chewing harder foods for at least 4 hours; no brushing teeth for at least 4 hours. Dental history to include previous adverse experiences with fluoride varnish and hypersensitivity/allergic reaction to colophony (natural resin) (p.5). No course duration is printed - each application is a single event; no first-line ranking is printed beyond 'the only fluoride varnish currently registered in Australia to prevent caries is Duraphat®'.

treatments.drug: Toothpaste (containing 500 to 550 ppm fluoride) - children aged 18 months to 5 years
treatments.notes: Preventative advice row, not a prescribed medicine (p.7, 'Provide general and preventative advice'): 'Teeth should be cleaned twice daily by a parent/caregiver with a pea sized amount of toothpaste (containing 500 to 550 ppm fluoride) using a small, soft bristled toothbrush. The child should be instructed to spit out, and not swallow the toothpaste, and not to rinse after brushing.' Transcribed exactly as printed; no unit normalisation.

treatments.drug: Toothpaste (containing 1000 to 1500 ppm fluoride) - people aged ≥6 years
treatments.notes: Preventative advice row, not a prescribed medicine (p.7, 'Provide general and preventative advice'): 'Teeth should be cleaned twice daily (or more frequently) with a soft bristled toothbrush and a toothpaste containing 1000 to 1500 ppm fluoride (a standard toothpaste readily available at supermarkets or the pharmacy). Toothpaste should not be swallowed, and the patient should avoid rinsing after brushing. Floss should be used to clean in between teeth. Plaque disclosing tablets may be used to demonstrate effective methods of plaque removal.' Transcribed exactly as printed.

open_questions.topic: Combinatorics of the eligibility checklist are inferred, not printed
open_questions.observed: 'Service recommended for patients aged 18 months and over', 'may only be used by pharmacists who...' and the consent/eligibility bullets imply AND for INC-1 to INC-4; p.3 'Patients may either be referred by a dental practitioner..., or assessed by the pharmacist...' introduces INC-5/INC-6 as alternatives, implying OR.
open_questions.why_unclear: The document never prints 'all of' or 'any of'; the all_of/any_of groups are inferred from the document's own framing per spec rule 4.

open_questions.topic: No action is stated for patients NOT screened at high or moderate risk
open_questions.observed: The flow gate for applying fluoride varnish is 'The patient is screened at high or moderate risk of tooth decay/poor oral health' (p.2, p.3, p.6). Nothing is printed for a patient assessed as low risk - no treatment and no referral.
open_questions.why_unclear: The gate on_fail is recorded as 'unclear' (PW-1-S4, PW-1-S6, PW-1-S8) rather than REFER or STOP, because the document is silent.

open_questions.observed: Referral destinations/triggers are printed on p.3 (Refer when / Treat and concurrently refer), p.4 (co-operation with visual screening), p.5 (doubt about suitability), p.9 (Appendix 1 tables) and p.11 (Appendix 3 tables), plus p.10 (mouth ulcers).
open_questions.why_unclear: Spec rule for the referral block: shared provenance uses the first page (page 3); the range 3-11 is recorded here.

open_questions.topic: Risk levels are qualitative labels with no scoring rule
open_questions.observed: 'There is no arbitrary scoring system for risk status due to the variability of the interaction between risk factors and protective factors. Pharmacists must use their professional judgement to evaluate a child's risk status.' (p.4). Appendix tables assign labels (Low/Moderate/Moderate to high/High) per row but print no total score, no cut-off and no rule for combining rows.
open_questions.why_unclear: Risk-level assignment cannot be encoded as a numeric rule from this document; row-level referral statements are captured verbatim in red_flags instead.

open_questions.topic: Age floor phrased differently in two places
open_questions.observed: p.1: 'Service recommended for patients aged 18 months and over'; p.4: 'Fluoride varnish should be considered for patients aged 18 months and over'; p.3: 'the patient is aged below 18 months' requires referral.
open_questions.why_unclear: The service is 'recommended' for 18 months and over while below 18 months is a referral trigger; age_bounds.min_years stored as 1.5 (18 months) because the schema requires years. The printed unit is months.

open_questions.topic: Adult dose (up to 0.75 mL) exceeds the single dose pack size (0.4 mL)
open_questions.observed: Appendix 4 doses: primary teeth only up to 0.25 mL; mixed dentition up to 0.4 mL; adolescents and adults with permanent dentition up to 0.75 mL (16.95 mg fluoride). The same appendix states 'A single use Duraphat® Dosage Pad ... or Duraphat® Varnish Single Dose (0.4 mL) must be used to ensure the correct amount of varnish is dispensed and applied', and equipment is 'single dose (0.4 ml) pack or multi dose tube'.
open_questions.why_unclear: The document does not say how a 0.75 mL adult dose is dispensed with a 0.4 mL single dose pack (two packs, or the multi dose tube); recorded as printed without reconciliation per spec rule 2.

open_questions.topic: The Refer when list is printed twice
open_questions.observed: The same triggers appear in the right-hand column of the Guideline overview on page 2 and again as the full 'Refer when' section on page 3, with matching wording.
open_questions.why_unclear: The list was captured once with provenance to page 3 (the dedicated section); the page 2 duplicates are noted here so the duplication is not lost.

open_questions.topic: Two risk assessment tools by age band
open_questions.observed: Appendix 1 is 'Risk assessment tool (18 months to 5 years)'; Appendix 3 is 'Risk assessment and screening tool ≥6 years'. Different risk factors and referral statements apply per band.
open_questions.why_unclear: Both tool tables are captured (RF-14 to RF-20 for 18 months to 5 years; RF-22 to RF-33 for ≥6 years); no tool covers a patient who is 5 years and some months turning 6 between assessments, which is not addressed.

open_questions.topic: No notifiable condition or statutory notification requirement printed
open_questions.observed: The guideline requires communication with other health practitioners and communication of the application to the patient's dental practitioner 'to avoid duplication of treatment', but mentions no notifiable condition, AIR notification or compulsory GP notification.
open_questions.why_unclear: notifiable.required is null because the document is silent.

open_questions.topic: No version number or date printed
open_questions.observed: No version, date, document ID or approving officer appears; page 15 shows footer codes "62'GUA" and "180510-DEC", 'Produced by Clinical Excellence Division' and '© Department of Health 2026'.
open_questions.why_unclear: instrument_version and effective_date cannot be populated beyond what is printed.

open_questions.topic: Source and adaptation acknowledged: originally Queensland Health material
open_questions.observed: Page 15: 'This document is based on clinical guidelines/protocols originally developed by Queensland Health for the Queensland Community Pharmacy Pilots.' Page 12: the Duraphat® application procedure 'is based on the Queensland Health Fluoride Varnish Guideline (QH-GDL-410:2013) and the Remote Primary Health Care Manual – Clinical Procedures Manual and has been contextualised for the community pharmacy setting'.
open_questions.why_unclear: Recorded for provenance of the instrument; no version of the Queensland originals is cited, so the WA document's own version cannot be derived from it.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm each pharmacist's EACPP approval and authorisation to prescribe under the Medicines and Poisons Regulations 2016 (WA), since 'This document alone does not provide an authorisation for a pharmacist to prescribe'.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Eligibility to use the guideline is conditional on departmental approval and authorisation that this document cannot evidence.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm the controlled version/date of this clinical practice guideline with the Department of Health (no version or date is printed; only footer codes "62'GUA" and "180510-DEC" and © Department of Health 2026).
hugh_to_confirm.reason: A clinical practice guideline used for funded prescribing must be version-controlled and traceable to an approval date.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm the local process for risk classification, since 'There is no arbitrary scoring system for risk status' and 'Pharmacists must use their professional judgement to evaluate a child's risk status'.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Risk level gates fluoride varnish application and referral, but no scoring rule or cut-off is printed; the judgement basis must be settled as local policy before go-live.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm which of the two printed tools applies operationally (Appendix 1 for 18 months to 5 years; Appendix 3 for ≥6 years), and how borderline patients are handled.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The tools carry different risk factors and different referral statements; a rules engine must know which table drives the check for a given patient.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm that Queensland Health Guideline for Fluoride Varnish (QH-GDL-410:2013) plus manufacturer product information remain the operative references for WA pharmacists checking contraindications, drug interactions and pregnancy/lactation - the guideline states 'General information only is provided within this guideline.'
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The core safety check for the procedure is delegated to an external Queensland document and product information; the cross-jurisdiction reference and currency (2013 guideline) must be verified for WA use.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm the referral destination logic when there is doubt about suitability: 'their preferred dental practitioner, closest public dental service, or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Community Controlled dental clinic'.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The choice among three destinations is left to the patient/pharmacist; local pathways and commissioning arrangements must be defined.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm the supply/frequency rules: twice per year, or up to 4 applications per year for patients at higher risk of dental caries, and how duplication with the patient's dental practitioner is avoided in practice.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Frequency is a printed recommendation but 'higher risk' is not numerically defined and the deduplication step depends on communication with an external dental provider.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm the dispensing arrangement for adult doses: up to 0.75 mL (16.95 mg fluoride) for adolescents and adults versus a stated single dose (0.4 mL) pack and dosage pad.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The document requires a single use dosage pad or single dose pack to be used for correct dosing but does not say how a 0.75 mL dose is measured; stock and dosing mechanics must be settled locally.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm community pharmacy equipment, PPE and procedure requirements in Appendix 4 (hand hygiene, PPE including gloves/eyewear/mask/apron, single use bib, positioning, quadrant isolation) as local policy.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The procedure 'has been contextualised for the community pharmacy setting' but local infection-control and stock requirements are left to the pharmacy.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm the action for a patient assessed as low risk (below high/moderate) - the document prints no treatment and no referral for this group.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The gate that fails for a low-risk patient has no documented on_fail action; it is recorded as 'unclear' in PW-1-S4/PW-1-S6.
